question: When was the James Webb Space Telescope launched, and what are three of its most important discoveries so far?

answer.text:
The **James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021**, at **7:20 a.m. EST (12:20 UTC)** aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. ([science.nasa.gov](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/webb/fact-sheet/?utm_source=openai))

Three of its most important discoveries so far are:

1. **A bright galaxy just 280 million years after the Big Bang.** Webb confirmed that **MoM-z14** existed remarkably early in cosmic history. Its brightness gives astronomers a concrete test of how quickly the first galaxies could form and grow. ([science.nasa.gov](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasa-webb-pushes-boundaries-of-observable-universe-closer-to-big-bang/?utm_source=openai))
2. **The first clear detection of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere.** In 2022, Webb identified CO₂ in the atmosphere of **WASP-39 b**, a hot gas giant, demonstrating how precisely it can measure the chemistry of planets around other stars. ([science.nasa.gov](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-detects-carbon-dioxide-in-exoplanet-atmosphere/?utm_source=openai))
3. **A previously unknown population of “little red dots” in the early universe.** Webb discovered these compact objects in 2022. Follow-up observations found strong evidence that at least one contains a rapidly growing supermassive black hole wrapped in dense gas, offering a clue to how black holes grew so early. ([science.nasa.gov](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/newfound-galaxy-class-may-indicate-early-black-hole-growth-webb-finds/?utm_source=openai))

3. A previously unknown population of “little red dots” in the early universe. Webb discovered these compact objects in 2022. report.answer_text:
The James Webb Space Telescope launched on December 25, 2021, at 7:20 a.m. EST (12:20 UTC) aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, French Guiana. (science.nasa.gov)
Three of its most important discoveries so far are:
1. A bright galaxy just 280 million years after the Big Bang. Webb confirmed that MoM-z14 existed remarkably early in cosmic history. Its brightness gives astronomers a concrete test of how quickly the first galaxies could form and grow. (science.nasa.gov)
2. The first clear detection of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere. In 2022, Webb identified CO₂ in the atmosphere of WASP-39 b, a hot gas giant, demonstrating how precisely it can measure the chemistry of planets around other stars. (science.nasa.gov)
3. A previously unknown population of “little red dots” in the early universe. Webb discovered these compact objects in 2022. Follow-up observations found strong evidence that at least one contains a rapidly growing supermassive black hole wrapped in dense gas, offering a clue to how black holes grew so early. (science.nasa.gov)

pages.quote_reason: The quote backs that a large fraction of little red dots show signs of growing supermassive black holes, but it does not say the growth is rapid or that it explains how black holes grew so early.
pages.page_reason: The page reports that about 70 percent of the sampled LRDs show fast-orbiting gas indicating growing supermassive black holes, and says this hints at an era of obscured black hole growth in the early universe, which broadly supports the claim that these objects offer a clue to early black hole growth.
